In-house exam

This is an image lab: expect a smear or marrow photo with a short history, asking for the diagnosis, the mechanism or the expected lab value. Work through the Slide ID drill until you can name each image cold.

LO 1Normal hematopoiesis and normal cells

Q1. How are red cells made?
  • Hematopoiesis: development of all blood cell lines; regulated by genes, the marrow microenvironment (stromal/supporting cells, proteins, cytokines) and growth factors
  • Pluripotential stem cells in marrow self-renew and differentiate along one line
  • Erythropoiesis is driven by erythropoietin; in adults it occurs in the marrow of the long bones, sternum and pelvis
  • As precursors mature, the nucleus shrinks and is ejected, and hemoglobin makes the cytoplasm pinker
Q2. What does a normal red cell and a normal smear look like?

Normal RBC

  • Biconcave disc, 6–9 µm across, 1.5–2.5 µm thick
  • No nucleus; flexible; full of hemoglobin
  • Dense pink rim, central pallor ≈ ⅓ of the cell
  • Uniformly pink cytoplasm, no inclusions
  • Minimal anisocytosis or poikilocytosis
Q3. What does normal bone marrow look like?

Look for

  • Megakaryocytes (large, lobulated)
  • Erythroid islands
  • Granulocytic precursors
  • = trilineage hematopoiesis
  • Fat mixed in: ≈50% cellular in middle age
  • Cellularity falls with age (high in children)
Memory tool

Rough rule: marrow cellularity ≈ 100 − age (%). A 50-year-old ≈ 50% cellular.

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A marrow biopsy from a 75-year-old is 25% cellular with normal trilineage cells. Abnormal?
No: cellularity falls with age (≈100 − age).

LO 2Classifying anemia

Q1. What do the key terms mean?
TermMeaning
Anemia↓ total RBCs, ↓ circulating hemoglobin, or ↓ RBC mass → reduced O₂ delivery
Peripheral smearA drop of blood spread on a slide; needed to assess morphology when labs are abnormal
MCVAverage RBC volume
MCHAverage Hb content per RBC
MCHCAverage Hb concentration in packed RBCs
RDWCoefficient of variation of RBC volume (size variation)
AnisocytosisVariation in size
PoikilocytosisVariation in shape
HypochromicLess Hb per cell → larger central pallor
HemoglobinopathyHereditary disease with structurally abnormal hemoglobin
Q2. How is anemia classified by MCV?
GroupMCVCommon causes
Microcytic<80 fLIron deficiency · thalassemia minor · anemia of chronic disease
Normocytic80–100 fLSickle cell · many hemolytic anemias · acute bleeding · chronic disease · marrow failure/infiltration
Macrocytic>100 fLMegaloblastic (B12, folate) · hemolytic anemias (retics) · liver and thyroid disease · primary marrow failure · drugs and toxins. Sub-classify by RDW and reticulocyte count

Common symptoms of any anemia: fatigue, headache, feeling cold.

Trap

This lab uses MCV <80 for microcytosis; the Anemia I lecture uses <70. If an in-house question gives an MCV between 70 and 80, read which lecture it comes from. Step 1 uses <80.

High yield

Always find the cause. A young woman's iron deficiency is not automatically menstrual; you can fix the iron level and miss a GI malignancy.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1Hb 9, MCV 112, retics 0.5%, hypersegmented neutrophils. Group and cause?
Macrocytic, megaloblastic (B12 or folate deficiency).

LO 3Mechanisms of each anemia

Q1. What causes iron deficiency anemia?
  • Causes: inadequate intake, poor absorption, blood loss
  • Sources: red meat, leafy green vegetables
  • Absorbed in the duodenum (and upper jejunum) → carried to marrow for Hb synthesis
  • Specific symptoms: pica, nail changes (koilonychia)
  • Most common cause of hypochromic microcytic anemia; highest risk in children and women of reproductive age (menses, pregnancy)
Q2. Why is β-thalassemia major so severe?
  • Quantitative hemoglobinopathy: ↓ or absent β-globin
  • Excess α chains aggregate → RBC membrane damage
  • Two mechanisms at once: ineffective erythropoiesis (precursors die in marrow) + extravascular hemolysis (splenic macrophages)
  • Result: severe microcytic anemia → marrow expansion into other bones including the skull; frequent transfusions → iron overload (secondary hemochromatosis)
Q3. What causes megaloblastic anemia?
  • B12 or folate deficiency: poor intake, poor absorption (including pernicious anemia), drug interference
  • Both are needed for DNA synthesis → the nucleus fails to mature or condense while the cytoplasm grows → macrocytosis
  • Pernicious anemia: autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → no B12 absorption → atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma
Q4. Why do sickle cells cause organ damage?
  • Qualitative hemoglobinopathy (HbSS); normocytic anemia
  • HbS crystallizes at low O₂ tension → long, thin sickle forms; triggers: hypoxia, infection
  • Sickling is reversible but damages the membrane → extravascular + intravascular hemolysis
  • Sticky sickled cells sludge and plug capillaries → ↓ flow → ischemia → autosplenectomy, femoral head avascular necrosis, painful crises
Q5. How are hemolytic anemias grouped?

Hemolysis = premature destruction of RBCs before ≈120 days.

Intrinsic vs extrinsic

  • Intrinsic (the RBC itself): hemoglobinopathies, cytoskeleton defects, enzyme deficiencies (G6PD)
  • Extrinsic: autoimmune, drugs, infection

Extravascular vs intravascular

  • Extravascular: splenic macrophages
  • Intravascular: e.g., mechanical cutting by fibrin strands → schistocytes

Consequences: ↑ RBC breakdown → ↑ bilirubin → jaundice; ↑ erythropoiesis → ↑ reticulocyte count.

Q6. What happens when the marrow itself fails or is replaced?
ConditionMechanism
Aplastic anemiaHematopoietic cells markedly reduced; causes: infection, drug, toxin; none found = idiopathic
Granulomatous marrowSmall, poorly formed granulomas (epithelioid macrophages); look for infection (cultures, special stains), Hodgkin lymphoma
Metastatic carcinomaCohesive clusters of epithelial cells replace hematopoietic cells (e.g., breast)

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1Which two processes make β-thalassemia major anemia so severe?
Ineffective erythropoiesis in the marrow + extravascular hemolysis in the spleen.
A2Why does pernicious anemia raise gastric cancer risk?
Autoimmune atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → intestinal-type adenocarcinoma.

Memory tool

Think in three windows: patient → blood → marrow. Every lab image question is asking you to fill in the missing window.

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A woman with lupus has jaundice and retics of 20%. Smear?
Spherocytes and bluish polychromatophilic reticulocytes (warm AIHA).

LO 5Smear and marrow atlas

Q1. What does iron deficiency look like?

Hypochromic microcytic

  • Small cells, bigger central pallor
  • ↑ anisocytosis and poikilocytosis

Iron deficiency

  • RBCs much smaller than the lymphocyte nucleus
  • Labs: ↓ ferritin, ↑ TIBC, ↑ RDW
Q2. What does β-thalassemia look like?

β-thalassemia

  • Marked poikilocytosis + anisocytosis
  • Microcytic; ineffective erythropoiesis
  • Labs: Hb electrophoresis (↑ HbF, ↑ HbA2)
Q3. What does megaloblastic anemia look like in blood and marrow?

Pernicious anemia

  • Hypersegmented neutrophil + macro-ovalocytes

Hypersegmented neutrophil

  • Up to 8 lobes instead of 3–4
  • Folate or B12 deficiency

Megaloblastic marrow

  • Enlarged nuclei in red cell precursors
  • Immature nuclear chromatin
  • Normal cytoplasm maturation without nuclear pyknosis
  • Nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony

Labs: ↓ B12 or folate; ↑ MMA (B12) and ↑ homocysteine; anti-IF / anti-parietal antibodies in PA.

Q4. What do sickle cells look like?

Sickle crisis

  • Long, thin sickle forms; sludge in capillaries

HbSS

  • Sickled cells stick together → ischemia (abdominal pain)
  • Labs: Hb electrophoresis (HbS)
Q5. What do the hemolytic anemias look like?

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

  • Small dense spherocytes (no pallor) + large bluish reticulocytes
  • Retics ≈20%; DAT positive

MAHA (DIC)

  • Fragmented RBCs = schistocytes, "helmet" cells
  • Labs: ↓ platelets, ↑ PT/PTT, ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ D-dimer (DIC)
Q6. Which other red cell findings should I know?

Malaria

  • Plasmodium ring forms inside RBCs (shown: P. vivax)
  • Four species infect humans; causes hemolysis and anemia

Rouleaux

  • RBCs stacked like coins
  • ↑ serum proteins (fibrinogen, globulins) → ↑ ESR
  • Classic in multiple myeloma
Step 1

Rouleaux = myeloma (M-spike). Agglutination (irregular clumps) = cold agglutinins. P. vivax/ovale have dormant liver hypnozoites → add primaquine (check G6PD first).

Q7. What do abnormal marrows look like?

Aplastic anemia

  • Hematopoietic elements markedly reduced; mostly fat
  • Infection, drug, toxin, or idiopathic

Marrow granuloma

  • Small, poorly formed; epithelioid macrophages
  • Cultures and special stains for infection; consider Hodgkin lymphoma

Metastatic carcinoma

  • Cohesive clusters of dark epithelial cells between trabeculae
  • Primary here: breast
Step 1

Marrow infiltration (myelophthisis) → leukoerythroblastic smear (immature WBCs + nucleated RBCs) and teardrop cells. Aplastic anemia → pancytopenia with no splenomegaly.

LO 6Treatment by anemia type

Q1. How is each anemia treated?
AnemiaTreatment
Iron deficiencyOral (or IV) iron; find and treat the cause (rule out GI cancer in adults)
Anemia of chronic diseaseTreat the underlying disease; EPO in some (e.g., CKD)
Thalassemia minorNo treatment; avoid unneeded iron; genetic counseling
β-thalassemia majorTransfusions + iron chelation; bone marrow transplant
B12 deficiency / PAParenteral (or high-dose oral) B12, lifelong in PA; screen for gastric cancer
Folate deficiencyOral folate; check B12 first
Sickle cellHydroxyurea (↑ HbF), hydration, pain control, vaccines/penicillin, transfusion, BMT
Warm AIHASteroids, IVIG; splenectomy; look for lupus/lymphoma
MAHA / DICTreat the cause; supportive blood products. TTP → plasma exchange
MalariaAntimalarials (by species and resistance)
Aplastic anemiaRemove offending drug/toxin; immunosuppression; stem cell transplant
Marrow infiltrationTreat the cancer or infection
In-house exam

The lab only asks you to briefly describe therapy. Pair each diagnosis with its one-line treatment, and remember: correct iron deficiency and find its cause.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A 34-year-old woman with fatigue has small red cells with enlarged central pallor and varied sizes. What is the most common cause of this picture?

Hypochromic microcytic anemia → iron deficiency most often.

2A smear shows a neutrophil with 8 nuclear lobes and large oval red cells. Which marrow finding is expected?

Megaloblastic marrow: nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony.

3A woman with lupus has jaundice, splenomegaly and a reticulocyte count of 20%. The smear shows small dense round cells without central pallor and large bluish cells. Diagnosis?

Spherocytes + reticulocytes + lupus → warm AIHA.

4A septic patient is bleeding from IV sites. The smear shows helmet-shaped red cell fragments. Diagnosis?

Schistocytes → MAHA; with sepsis and bleeding → DIC.

5A 70-year-old with bone pain and renal insufficiency has red cells stacked in long chains. Which serum protein change explains this?

Rouleaux from ↑ globulins/fibrinogen → classic in multiple myeloma; raises ESR.

6A traveler returning from Asia has fevers and anemia. The smear shows small rings inside red cells. Diagnosis?

Plasmodium ring forms → malaria, causing hemolysis.

7A patient with pancytopenia after a toxin exposure has a marrow biopsy showing mostly fat and very few hematopoietic cells. Diagnosis?

Markedly reduced hematopoietic elements = aplastic anemia (infection, drug, toxin, idiopathic).

8A woman with a history of breast cancer has new anemia. Her marrow shows cohesive clusters of dark blue cells between bony trabeculae. Diagnosis?

Cohesive epithelial clusters replacing marrow = metastatic carcinoma (myelophthisic anemia).

9Which two mechanisms combine to cause the severe anemia of β-thalassemia major?

Precipitated α chains → precursors die in marrow + splenic removal of damaged RBCs.

10A 10-year-old with HbSS has severe abdominal pain. The smear shows long, thin, curved cells. Which mechanism explains the pain?

HbS crystallizes at low O₂ → sickle cells sludge in capillaries → ischemia.

11Which term describes variation in red cell shape?

Poikilocytosis = shape; anisocytosis = size.

12A 25-year-old woman has iron deficiency anemia and heavy periods. Iron replacement works, but what else is essential?

Don't assume menstruation: correct the iron and look for other causes such as GI bleeding or malignancy when the story doesn't fit.
